Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 114, to amend the Indian Act.
He said: The object of this Bill is to amend the Indian Act in several particulars. At the present time Indian children can only be sent to industrial schools. We wish to amend .the Act to give us authority to declare a school an industrial school in provinces where there are no industrial schools. Another amendment is in reference to securing sites for schools and enlarging the present sites. There has been some difficulty in the past in securing sites and in enlarging the present grounds. This amendment will give us power to secure a certain portion of the reserves for school sites, and will decide how compensation shall be made. Another amendment provides for the administration of the estates of deceased Indians. It extends the Act's application to cases where no widow or minor children are left. We are also amending the Act of 1911, which gave the -Government power to expropriate Indian reserves adjacent to towns of 8,000 population or over, when such lands were required -for public purposes, and the Indians Tefused to surrender them. These cases are disposed of by the Exchequer -Court. This amendment extends the application of that Act to lands which are not necessarily adjacent to a town of 8,000 population. Another amendment is in reference to sanitary regulations on the reserves, to prevent outbreaks of contagious and infectious diseases. Another amendment is to prevent Indians selling immature thoroughbred cattle supplied to them by the department. At present some of the Indians sell these animals without the knowledge of the Indian agent. The purchasers, however, are liable to have the animals confiscated.
They cannot sell without the consent of the agent?

They do sell without the consent of the agent, and this is to make selling prohibitive except with the agent's consent. Another amendment is to prevent the participation of Indians in dances or stampedes outside their own reserve without the consent of the Indian agent. This privilege has been abused in the past, and we find it advisable to restrict it. The last amendment is in reference to a half-breed withdrawing from a treaty. At present a separate application is required for a wife to withdraw, but under this amendment the wife withdraws without separate application.
Motion agreed -to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These are the only provinces where drifting for salmon is practised; in the other provinces, salmon are caught in fixed nets. In the bay of Fundy, because of the great rise and fall of the tide, it is impossible to set nets, and so salmon are caught by drifting.

On section 31-fishways to be made as fishery officer directs:

I wish to call to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries a matter pertinent to this section. I am very much interested in the preservation of the statutory rights which will ensure, by the use of fishways or other means, the passage of fish up our rivers. But conditions are sometimes found on small rivers where for a great number of years there have been small mills with dams, and where there never have been fishways, and I think the minister should exercise his powers rather carefully in such cases.
A case of that kind exists in my own county on the river John, which empties into the strait of Northumberland. At some distance up the river there has been, so long as I can remember-and I have very often, in my younger days, fished below the dam-a mill known as Weir's mill, where a dam has existed for forty or fifty years. This mill is only a small one, but it has been a convenience for the farmers in that locality. It is now proposed in some quarter or other that a fishway should be placed in the dam. In the first place, I do not think there is any great demand for it from anybody who is interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What fish are in the river now?
Trout.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No salmon?

Mr. Hockin the inspector of fisheries in the district, has impressed upon the proprietor the fact that he must put in a fishway. It will be a great expense to do so, because on one side of the river there is a very precipitous rocky bank and on the other bank, closely adjacent to the dam, is the mill itself. I have a petition addressed to the minister, which I will send to him, signed by fifty farmers in the district who patronize this mill. A number of heirs have titles to the land, and a person is operating the mill. If any advantage from a fishing standpoint would ensue, I would urge the minister to exercise his authority and have a fishway put in, because I often go fishing below the dam when I have the opportunity. I have no fault to find with the provisions of the statute, but I call the attention of the minister to this particular case, and ask him to exercise his discretion and say that in this case there is no necessity for a fishway. My reasons are that no salmon have ever been known to go up the river John; that the mill has been there for so long, and that conditions generally are such that it seems that at this late date it would impose a very great cost on the owner of the mill with no great benefit to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The provisions of a statute of this kind should be enforced with discretion and good judgment. Unless it were in the public interest that this fishway should be put in, there would be no reason for causing expense and annoyance to any owner of a dam on the river. I will give every attention to the petition which my hon. friend is going to send to me, and
have this matter carefully investigated before any action is taken. Subsection 4 of this section reads as follows:
The minister may authorize the payment of one-half of the expenses incurred by such owner or occupier in constructing: and maintaining any fish-way or canal.
If it be found necessary to put in a fishway here in the interest of the preservation of fish, it seems to be a place where the department ought to pay a share of the cost, because that dam has existed for so many years without hindrance. There is another paragraph in the section which provides:
After a fishway or canal, which has been virtually approved by the department, has been changed at the cost of the. owner or occupier, or after he has paid one-half of the cost, if it is found that it does not prove effective, then the total cost of any change in such fishway, in order to make it effective, will be paid by His Majesty.
That is only right and proper. That provision did not exist before because fishways which had been put in and approved by officials of the department and had later been found to be ineffective were ordered to be changed and the owner of the dam had to pay the cost. This provides that if these fishways are approved by the department and afterwards, on being found to be ineffective, are changed, then the department has to pay the cost.

I am very much
obliged for the promise of the minister to look into the matter. No .salmon have gone up the river John within my recollection.
Perhaps I might venture to take the opportunity of calling to the attention of the minister the conditions existing in our county with reference to the poaching carried on in the larger rivers where there are no dams to prevent the salmon from going up. The salmon industry along Northumberland strait from Pictou harbour extending to Arisaig is a very profitable one in the summer season for a large number of people. Great complaints are being made by them on account of the uncertainty rf the industry and the danger of the salmon being depleted, which they attribute largely to the fact that poaching has been carried on to an indiscriminate extent in the rivers that flow into Northumberland strait at these points. I would ask the .minister to take up the question seriously as to whether some more rigid method * can not be devised to prevent this poaching from going on. Some people of the greatest respectability, who, one would

think, would he the last persons in the world to poach, regularly make it their business in the months of October and November to lay in a supply of salmon when the salmon are going up the river to spawn. The result is that in these rivers, whereas a few years ago we were able to catch salmon in the season, we are now unable to catch them at all. It is having an effect upon the industries lying near the mouths of these rivers owing to the theory that the salmon returns to its particular river to spawn. We have been appointing guardians for years, but their operations do not seem to be effective. Whether better results would be obtained if the people who were so employed did not live in the particular districts along the river, I do not know. I am quite sure the minister is seized of the condition of affairs to which I refer; I speak on behalf of those whose earnings are very seriously affected by the depletion or increase of salmon. I would suggest that the minister give his serious attention to this matter with a view of adopting the most stringent methods to stop poaching, not only in the interests of those who make their living out of the industry, but in the interests of those who love the sport of fishing, and also find that salmon fishing has almost become a thing of the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The report made to me by the Superintendent of Fisheries is that year by year the fishery protection is becoming better in all the districts in the Maritime provinces, with the exception of one district, which I need not mention, but which we are taking steps to improve. In the bay of Fundy the salmon are increasing to such an extent that it is being represented to us that the salmon go up a number of the rivers discharging into the bay until they come to dams or other obstructions, and can go no further. This is taking place now to a much greater extent than it did a few years ago. There is no doubt that the waters of the bay of Fundy contain a large supply of salmon; such a thing as a failure of catch has not been known for a number of years. I attribute that very largely to the fact that year by year the fishery regulations are being better enforced, and that artificial propagation is having a very beneficial effect. I do not know whether or not the rivers mentioned by the hon. member for Pictou are being replenished by artificial propagation; if they are not, it seems to me that steps should be taken not only to afford better protection but also to see that every year some salmon

fry are placed in those waters, so that there will be an increase in the supply of salmon in the future. If these salmon resort to the rivers mentioned by my hon. friend to spawn, then it is important that any obstructions which prevent them from getting to a natural spawning bed should be removed. I shall have very great pleasure in referring the matter mentioned by my hon. friend to the fishery officers of the department, and in asking them to give it their serious attention with a view to trying to improve existing conditions.

Yes, that would be a
matter of regulation for this Parliament.
Have any representations been made to the Government in regard to allowing the marketing of whitefish ox a smaller size than those that have been marketed in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The licenses which are
issued by the Ontario Government restrict the size of the whitefish that can be taken to two pounds, but the superintendent of fisheries has been urging upon the Govern^
merit of Ontario a revision of these regulations and of the provision inserted in their licenses to fish in their lakes and rivers.

Some representations
have been made to me in regard to this matter which appeal to me quite strongly.
I can understand having regulations stating, for instance, that whitefish less than two pounds in weight should not be exported. But some people have been urging that the .law should be a little freer in regard to the marketing of whitefish within the bounds of the respective provinces. It is urged that where whitefish are caught in Ontario, or in Quebec, the people should have the right to market fish of a smaller size within the bounds of the province than they would be permitted to export. If the regulation was that they should not export any whitefish under two pounds in weight the .suggestion is that they might be allowed to sell within the bounds of the province wherein the fish were caught, whitefish of less than two pounds in weight. That appeals very strongly to me as being quite a reasonable proposition. I know of some places where there are thousands of fish that will go a pound and a half in weight but do not seem to put on the other half pound for some reason or other. I know of one firm that obtained fishing rights on lake Manitou who spent thousands of dollars in putting in their appliances for carrying on the industry, fish hatchery, boats and nets, and they are unable to make anything out of their fish because they seem to run at a weight of about a pound and a half. They cannot get them in sufficient numbers weighing two pounds, as called for by the regulations, to make it profitable. If the regulation permitted them to market these fish in the province in which they were caught and did not insist upon a weight of two pounds, they might be able to carry on a more profitable business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The size of the fish that
may be sold is governed by the regulation with regard to the .size of the mesh which can be used for catching fish of this sort. I understand the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards), but I would point out that there are interior lakes in the province in which the fish are not so large as in the Great Lakes; and, while the two-pound limit for the Great Lakes might be proper, it would not suit those other waters. The policy we have been pursuing for the ilast few years is always to consult the
Ontario Government before making regulations in connection with the fisheries over which they are the proprietary owners. The matter mentioned by my hon. friend is worthy of consideration, and we will take it up in the department with the view of providing some reasonable regulation.
Is there not an international understanding with regard to the weight or size of fish which may be caught?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not yet. Under the provisions of the treaty between the two countries *a commission was appointed -by the United States and by Canada to frame regulations for the control of the fisheries in waters contiguous to the international boundary line. That commission framed regulations, and in 1910, under the provisions of the treaty, this Parliament passed the necessary legislation making then effective. The United States has not yet passed concurrent legislation. The matter is now before the Congress and we will know in a few days whether that legislation will be passed or not. We gave notice to the United States some time ago, that unless their legislation was passed by the first of March of this year, we would resume our liberty of action, as we felt we had waited- long enough. About the first of March, the United States Senate passed the legislation necessary, and it was sent to the House of Representatives. We were asked if under those circumstances, we would stick literally to the first of March, and we answered that we were prepared to wait a reasonable time, if the matter were seriously taken up.
Does this Bill regulate the size of fish to be caught in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have full power here to pass regulations controlling the fisheries, but as Ontario has taken over the administration of its fisheries, it has a proprietary right in them. Before promulgating regulations under this Act we consult with the provincial department of fisheries.
The different states in the United States, seem to have power to make fishery regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have, and that is why a treaty was necessary.
I am personally cognizant of the fact that Michigan, New York, and Illinois, each has its regulations, and these regulations differ in each state as to the catching and marketing of white-fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is right.

Fish will lose about twenty-five per cent of their weight between the time they are taken from the water and the time they are placed on the market; does the two-pound 'limit apply to freshly caught fish, or, to fish when offered for sale?	i

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The provision in the license issued by the Government of Ontario is, that the fish when taken from the water should weigh not less than two pounds.

If these international
fishery regulations come into effect, would they regulate the size of the fish and the size of the mesh, or would that still be under the jurisdiction of this Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The regulations, if they do come into effect, provide for the size of the mesh, and they will abolish a certain description of traps which are largely used on the American side of lake Erie. The necessity for a treaty is, that in the United States each state controls its own fisheries, and the states along the Great Lakes have different regulations, so that when we endeavoured to have uniform regulations on both sides of the boundary, we found it impossible to deal with each state separately. Consequently, a treaty was entered into in 1908, under which the matter can be dealt with from the standpoint of the United States as a whole. It was set out in the treaty to be the duty of each government to pass the necessary legislation to make the regulations effective. This Parliament, in 1910, took the view that it was not for it to criticise the regulations decided upon by the International Commission, and without any discussion on their merits, Parliament, acting as I think it was in honour bound to act under the treaty, passed the required legislation. Up to the present time, the United States has not done so. When President Taft sent his message to Congress, it went to the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, and lobbyists came to Washington, representing fishery interests on the Pacific coast, on lake Michigan, and other parts of the country, protesting against the passing of the legislation to make this treaty effective, on the ground that it prejudicially affected their interests. In my opinion that was a most improper course, but it was a course that probably could not be prevented, because under the constitution of the United States the President has no means, even after a treaty has been entered into, of

forcing the Congress to pass legislation to make it effective. The Government of Canada agreed to certain modifications as to the size of the nets to be used on lake Michigan. I saw President Wilson with regard to the matter, and he told me that as the last session of the Congress was a tariff session, called for the special purpose of dealing with the tariff, it was impossible to take a question of this kind up for consideration, thoueb he expressed his entire sympathy with the treaty and his desire to have it made effective. Therefore we passed an Order in Council, which was communicated to the Government of the United States, stating distinctly that, unless the United States -by the 1st of March of the present year passed the necessary legislation in order to make the treaty effective, we would be compelled to resume our liberty of action. We felt that, four years having elapsed from the time those resolutions were promulgated, we should not wait any longer for the action of the .United States. The matter came before the Senate committee again at this session, and legislation was passed there. A Bill was also introduced into the House of Representatives; but representatives of people interested in the fisheries of lake Erie on the United States side protested against the passing of the regulations on the ground that these regulations did an injury to fishermen on the American side of the line. We were asked if we would agree to a modification of the regulations, and we distinctly but respectfully declined to do so. We said that we felt we should stand by the treaty; but if, after legislation to make the treaty effective was passed in the United States, it was found that these regulations were not in the interest of the fisheries, we were willing to have the matter further considered by the commission, and any injustice that might result might be removed by consent of the commissioners and of both countries. The matter is still before the House of Representatives. Although we had stated that we would resume our liberty of action on the 1st of March, we were asked if we would literally stand by that; and, in view of the fact that the matter was actually under consideration by the Congress of the United States, we said that, as the matter was now being considered in good faith, we would not stand literally by that statement, and no doubt in a few days it will be determined
whether the Congress of the United States is going to pass legislation to make this treaty effective ot not. If it does not do so, the treaty is at an end.
It is most unfortunate that different regulations should exist on the two sides of the boundary line. We are enforcing strictly the laws with regard to close seasons and the kind of nets to be used in catching fish, and our fishermen see the American fishermen come up to the international boundary line and fish without let or hindrance during the whole year. It rather enrages our fishermen to think that while we in Canada are spending money for the artificial propagation of fish in the Great Lakes, increasing the number of the fish and protecting the fish by regulations, a protection which inures equally to the advantage of the fishermen on the American side of the boundary line, the fishermen on the other side are allowed to fish without the control which exists on the Canadian side. If the treaty is not confirmed by the United States, the question will arise as to whether we shall continue to enforce on the -uanadian side of the line the regulations we are now enforcing, or whether we shall follow the example of the United States, which, in the opinion of our fishery officers, is detrimental to the fish in those lakes. I thought well to give this explanation to the House in view of what my hon. friend said. I presume it will be only a matter of a day or two until we shall know whether the regulations will be made effective or not.

Will my hon. friend be good enough to consider the question which concerns us in northern central Ontario? We are not vitally interested in this boundary question or in the Great Lakes question, but we are very deeply concerned in what one might call the fisheries of the minor inland waters. All through the Trent and Muskoka districts are a large number of small lakes ranging from
3,000	to 15,000 acres in extent. They usually run one into the other and are a perfect paradise for the angler. A great many American and Canadian tourists visit these districts and are directly or indirectly interested in these inland fisheries, and the people there are constantly making inquiries as to where they .shall apply to have these waters replenished. At various times I have endeavoured to find out what I might call a settled and regular way of having this question answered. Thanks to the courtesy of the Department
of Marine and Fisheries I have found out a good deal, but not enough to satisfy the_ people living beside these waters. For example, they do not understand the difference between the provincial jurisdiction and the Dominion jurisdiction. When they ask a question and are told to apply to the province for an answer, they write to the province and are told to apply to the Dominion. That happens in very many cases. The consequence is that they are in an unsettled state, which they feel is greatly to their prejudice. This is a matter the importance of which is out of all proportion to the intrinsic value of the fish. As the people connected with this pursuit are usually wealthy, it is an important industry for the people in these districts. In regard to the fish hatcheries, they want to know who will establish them. I tell them that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries attends to commercial fish, but not to game fish. Then they ask me to find out what fish are commercial fish and what are game fish. I cannot tell them, because it would take six months for me to get that question settled. Then they write to the provincial Government. If the minister will say how far he will interfere in seeing that the waters are replenished and with what fish, and what he will do in the way of fish hatcheries for us, he will confer a great favour not only on me but on a large number of people in those districts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Government of Canada, as far as fish hatcheries are concerned in the province of Ontario, confine itself to the propagation of commercial fish. Sporting fish are looked after by the province. From what my hon. friend says, I judge that in the lakes to which he refers, the fish that the tourists want are trout and other sporting fish. If that is so, my hon. friend and his friends will have to take the matter up with the Government of Ontario, who have taken over the administration of the fish in that province as they have a perfect right to do. As they have done that, the agreement has been come to that we shall simply look after the propagation of commercial fish. The confusion that my hon. friend refers to as having occurred is quite natural in view of the dual control of the fish, which, under the decision of the courts, unfortunately exists.

I hope that the minister
will give very serious consideration to the question of this international fish treaty with the United States, especially as to making any modification or change in it. I recognize that the Government of this coun-

try are committed by their representative on the commission to a treaty with the United States.
I had the pleasure a few days ago of taking a large delegation from my county to Toronto to meet the Minister of Marine and Fisheries regarding certain regulations. We were informed by the minister that those regulations were made by the Dominion, and that the provincial Government carried them out. On lake Erie, under the new treaty, there will be a uniform size of mesh on both sides of the lake; but it is a fact, as stated by this delegation of fishermen, that certain different families of fish seem to locate in different sections of the lake. For instance, at Port Maitland, in my county, the whitefish they catch are entirely different from the whitefish caught at Port Dover, twenty miles to the west. There they catch a much smaller white-fish than we do, and the mesh they use would be entirely too small to catch white-fish at Port Maitland. The opposite applies to herring; at Port Maitland they are very much smaller than they are twenty miles west. The meshes used to catch herring in those districts could not be used near Port Maitland; the fish would simply go through them. It has been represented by our fishermen to me and to the Ontario Government, through the delegate to which I have referred, that if these proposed regulations go into effect and a mesh of the size prescribed is used, the fishermen along the shore of lake Erie will practically have to go out of business. My opinion is that any provision for the use of meshes of a uniform size on lake Erie is not practicable, because of the different families of fish, of different sizes, which apparently abound in various parts of the lake. From the representations which have been made to me, I doubt very much whether this International Fisheries Treaty is in the interests of Canada, and I hope the Government will go very slowly in carrying its regulations into effect unless they believe they will accrue to the advantage of cur Canadian fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This, treaty was entered into in 1908; the regulations were promulgated by the commissioners in 1910, and this Parliament passed legislation to make them effective. If the United States passes similar legislation, there is no course open to the Government but to carry those regulations into effect. I understand that the treaty provides that its terms shall continue in force for a period of four years from the time they come into effect, and

that upon one year's notice they can be abrogated. If the United States agrees to these regulations the Government of Canada will have to carry out in good faith the regulations drawn up by Professor Prince on behalf of Canada and by Professor Starr Jordan on behalf of the United States. I presume that these commissioners, being experts, have considered very carefully the effect of the regulations. There may be cases in which the new regulations may be against the interests of the United States; there may be otner cases where they are unfavourable to Canada, but, taken as a whole, it is believed that the regulations will be in the interests of the preservation of fish and, in the end, very much in the interests of the fisherrden, whose welfare depends so largely upon an abundant supply of fish every year.

I fully recognize that if the regulations are accepted by the United States, the Canadian Government is committed to the terms of the treaty, but I merely want to draw the attention of the minister to some of the objectionable features of it, in order that he may keep them in view in case the treaty is not accepted by the United States in its present form. Does the treaty provide that whitefish may not be caught in lake Erie after November 15 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Has the hon. minister in mind any method by which he can ascertain whether or not the fishery officers are performing their duties fairly and impartially?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We get reports from the inspector of fisheries for the district; if we want further information about any individual we communicate with that official.

In the case of a report coming to the department that an officer is not properly carrying out his duties, would the minister consider it advisable to send into the district in question some person "who is not connected with the department, and whose purpose would be to inquire as to the truth of the report? I would point out that when a person who is known to be an officer of the department puts in an appearance, everybody is on his good behaviour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman would suggest the employment of a detective to visit the different districts.

Yes, practically so-a
man in plain clothes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has been necessary in some eases to send special officers to the district to investigate charges that have been made; the whole matter is one of policy, as to what is the right thing to do in a particular case under consideration. Complaints have been made to the department at different times, and officers have been sent out without the officials in the district being aware that they were being sent to investigate and report. I presume the same policy will continue in the future. As to employing a sort of Pinkerton man to go round among the fishery officers and lay complaints against them, I think the ease would have to be a rather strong one before we would be Justified in taking any such course as that.

I think it desirable
that fishery officers should be located as near the scene of their duties as possible.
I know of certain districts in and around the Island of Cape Breton the officers in charge of which live quite a distance away, and are, perhaps, not seen in the district in question more than two or three times a week. I am particularly interested in angle fishing; I love the sport very much. There are many beautiful streams for trout fishing in the counties of Victoria and Inverness, and people come there with nets at all hours of the night and sometimes during the day, while the guardians who are appointed to look after the streams are miles away, and never come near the place at all. I hope the minister will see that the persons who are appointed to carry out these duties are capable and competent persons, and that they shall live within a reasonable distance of the place in which their duties are to be discharged.
I wish to avoid troubling the minister when the Bill comes up for a third reading. Section 85 presents the same difficulty that I spoke of yesterday, that is, the appointment of a fishery officer as a justice of the peace. Yesterday, I, with other hon. gentlemen, protested against this as strongly as we could, and I wish to say a little more about it to-day. I wish to put the responsibility entirely upon the shoulders of the minister. I shall not lay down any positive idea or opinion of what our powers are in respect to the making of appointments of this kind, that is, the appointment of a stipendiary magistrate or a justice of the peace, but it would appear to me that the appointment of magistrates and the creation of courts of a 1 kinds with few exceptions, are vested in the UC
provincial legislatures, and we should keep as far from trenching upon their jurisdiction as possible. Sub-section 27 of section 91 of our constitution says:
The criminal law, except the constitution of the courts of criminal jurisdiction, but including the procedure in criminal matters-
-shall be within the powers of this Parliament. That is, the constitution or creation of courts with criminal jurisdiction is not within our power at all; yet, here, in this very Act, section 85, we are creating a court that has criminal jurisdiction, because we are providing for the punishment of certain offences, and we create a court to try them. Section 92 says:
The administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts, both of civil and criminal jurisdiction, and including procedure in civil matters in those courts-
-shall be absolutely within the powers of the provinces. That is our constitution, that the creation of courts, both civil and criminal, shall be within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and only when necessity arises, should we depart from that principle and try to get power to create those courts.
I think it would be well to stand by the constitution.
I submit further to the minister that at common law any decision given by such a court as he is creating would not stand the test for one minute. This officer cannot possibly be regarded as free from suspicion of bias. All that the common law requires to set aside a conviction made by any inferior court is that the possibility of bias shall be present. How can the minister say that an overseer, who lias a staff of officers under him in the shape of guardians to set aside a conviction made by any inferior court, and whose duty it is to see that these guardians do their duty, that duty being to catch and punish poachers, can be regarded as free from the possibility of bias in trying a person brought in by one of his subordinates on a charge of having violated the regulations which it is the duty of the fishery overseer to enforce? Not only does the law require that there shall be proof of bias,
5	p.m. but if the possibility of bias is present the conviction would not stand for a minute. I wish to quote a few sentences from Tremeear's Criminal Law, volume 11, page 125:
To invalidate the conviction on the ground of bias in the convicting magistrate, it is not necessary that actual bias should be proved, and



a conviction will be quashed if the facts justify a reasonable apprehension of bias.
That is all that is necessary. If my hon. friend were sitting as a judge, hearing an application to quash a conviction, and the facts were that an officer of the department, whose duty it was to suppress poaching, had sent out a subordinate, and that subordinate had brought in a man caught poaching, and the fishery officer was immediately called upon to try the prisoner, would my hon. friend say that there was not the possibility of bias? This writer goes on:
If the accused is aware of the disqualifying circumstances at the time of the hearing before the magistrate, he should take objection then to the magistrate acting.
Where the prosecutor in summary proceedings is the magistrate's father, and the statute under which the prosecutor is brought entitles the prosecutor to a share of any fine imposed, the justice is disqualified from adjudicating upon the case.
A conviction made under oucii circumstances will be quashed, although there was no conflicting evidence on the summary trial.
A magistrate is disqualified from trying an information for an offence punishable on summary conviction where there is a bona fide action pending against him brought by the husband of the accused for alleged malicious conduct as a judicial officer and for assault. If the action against the justice is not bona fide but a mere sham to attempt to disqualify him, its pendency will not operate as a disqualification. The principles which govern the the challenge of a juryman for favour are applicable to the disqualification of a justice on the ground of bias.
That is, if a man is disqualified from being a juror, he is also disqualified from trying the case as a court himself. I am sure my hon. friend will at once agree that if a man should be brought up to be tried by a jury, one of those guardians who arrested him would not be regarded as a qualified juror, nqr would the overseer who sent out the guardian to make the arrest. On the same ground I submit that the overseer should not be created a court by the minister or by this House. (Reading):
A magistrate who is engaged in the same kind of business as a trader prosecuted under a transient trader's license law is hereby disqualified from adjudicating upon the charge.
For instance, a grocer would not be permitted to sit upon the trial of another man charged with selling groceries as a transient trader without a license, 'because there might me some possibility that he would be prejudiced against the prisoner. (Reading):
Justices of the peace, who belong to an association (a temperance alliance) of which [Mr. McKenzie 1
the president is the party prosecuting, and to which association any fine to be imposed upon the accused for the offence against the liquor law with which he is charged would be paid under resolution of the municipal council, are disqualified from trying the charge, and will be prevented by a writ of prohibition from so doing. The fact that between the time when the information was received by such justices and the hearing of the charge, the justices had withdrawn from the association does not validate the proceedings.
This shows the extreme sensitiveness with which the highest authorities view cases of this kind. Here is a case of a man who was simply a member of a temperance society. Before he tried the case he resigned, but the mere fact that he took information before he resigned rendered his decision invalid, and it was set aside by the higher court. These cases-and they are backed up by English decisions by the score-show that if there is the slightest possibility of a biased decision, that decision goes by the board.
I therefore submit that it is an impossibility for the minister, by any legislation in this House, to take away the powers of the courts to set aside the decisions that might be rendered by any of his officials acting as judges. And now that the matter has been brought to his attention, I submit that it would be unwise legislation, and flying in the face of decisions of our highest courts, to try to create a court by any enactment of this House that would not be in harmony with our ideas of the administration of justice, particularly of criminal justice. These are matters which I intended at a later date to bring to the notice of the minister and the House. But I took the opportunity of submitting the facts on this section, and I leave the responsibility entirely with the minister to decide whether it is wise, in view of the authorities I have quoted, and in view of what was said in his presence yesterday, still to persist in making those officials, who must necessarily be interested in their own prosecutions, judges, with power to fine and imprison people because they do something which these so-called judges are paid for preventing.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have listened with
interest to the arguments advanced by my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman says he proposes to leave the responsibility with me; I am quite willing to take that responsibility. This section is not a new one: I am not making any new law, but am simply re-enacting what has been the law Of this country for a considerable
number of years. While I do not propose to enter into an argument on constitutional grounds, it appears to me that if this Parliament had not the power to pass that legislation, it would have been attacked long ago, and it would have been decided by- some court of competent authority that it was ultra vires of this Parliament, and any convictions that might have been made, under the provisions of this Act to which my hon. friend objects, would have been set aside. As I pointed out to this House yesterday, there are places in Alberta and Saskatchewan, and certain out-of-the-way parts of Canada, where it would be impossible to enforce the law at all, were it not for these provisions; or we should have to pay the expenses of those who were found violating this law for travelling perhaps a hundred, miles, in order to find a justice of the peace who had the 'authority to try the offences laid against them. Under these circumstances I am prepared to take the full responsibility of having this legislation passed by this Parliament. If it is ultra vires of this Parliament, it is open to anybody Who is accused of an offence under the provisions of any of these sections to appeal from that decision and to get a judgment as to whether or not we have that authority. But I am not prepared to agree to the doctrine that we have not authority to pass a law which has been for many year9 the law of the land, until a decision to the contrary has been given by some court having jurisdiction in this matter.

I do not feel strongly as to whether or not this Parliament has the power to appoint a person in the capacity of a justice of the peace to try summarily offences under the provisions of this Act. I am rather of the opinion, however, that this Parliament has that power. Undoubtedly, as the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has argued, if any conviction made. by a fisheries officer, acting in the capacity of a justice of the peace, were attacked on the ground of bias, the offender could have the decision tested in a higher court. I would like to point out to the minister that in connection with subsection 2 of section 5, it is necessary to have the authority of the Governor in Council to make an official a justice of the peace. The minister will, of course, exercise, great discretion when considering upon whom he will confer this power. If I am right with 116}
reference to subsection 2 of section 5, I think there should also be an amendment to section 87, adding the words, 'who is so authorized by the Governor in Council.'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite right, and I accept that at once.

I think there 13 a good deal in what the minister has said in reference to the length of time the law has been in force. I think, however, that the minister should be very cautious in conferring the powers of a justice of the peace on fishery officers generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the point is correctly taken by my hon. friend, and . I would like to amend this section by adding after the words 'fishery officer,' at the end of the third line, the following words: 'who is authorized by the Governor in Council to exercise the powers of a justice of the peace.'

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 93-appeal in case of grievance by conviction:
I would like to ask the minister if, under the old Act, the right of appeal was taken away?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There was no right of appeal under the old Act to a judge of the county court; the only right of appeal was to the minister.

Was the question
brought up by any member of the committee as to whether or not this language is strong enough to allow an appeal? It says:
Nothing in this section contained shall prevent any person who thinks himself aggrieved by any such conviction or order or dismissal, the prosecutor or complainant, as well as the defendant, from any right of appeal that he may have under the provisions of Part XV of the Criminal Code.
I am not very well versed in the law with regard to this particular question, but it struck me that the language was not sufficiently explicit.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The section was drafted
by. the Parliamentary counsel, Mr. Gisborne, and I presume he considered it sufficient.

I forget whether the
statute requires that the appeal shall be granted by direct assumption or whether it

shall be granted by imputation as it is here.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the right of appeal must have been taken away by the old section.

I would infer that the'
right of appeal must be given in the statute. There was no appeal, I know, under the old statute.
The proceedings aTe under the Summary Convictions Act.

My hon. friend from
North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) states that there is a right of appeal unless it is expressly taken away.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, that makes it all
right.
The appeal was taken away by the Fisheries Act.

Section agreed to.
On section 46 -fishery officer may convict on view:
This gives the right to a fishery officer, acting as a justice of the peace, to convict ' on view.' I think it is a most unheard of thing. I do not know that it has ever been exercised.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This has been the law for many years and I have never heard of any complaint under it.

I have never heard of
it being exercised.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Probably it never has been.
I think it would be better to allow it to pass now and if the hon. gentleman wants to take it up again he may do so on the third reading.

Section agreed to.
On section 17-as to spawning rivers:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) raised a point in regard to section 17 and we left it over for consideration. It provides for:
No salmon shall be fished for, caught or killed otherwise than by angling with hook and line within two hundred yards of the mouth of any tributary, of any ereek or stream which salmon frequent to spawn.
Upon thinking the matter over, it seems to me that if, in the absence of authority,
I were asked to give a judgment as to what that meant, I should say that it meant two hundred yards in any direction

two hundred yards along the shore to the right, two hundred yards along the shore to the left, or two hundred yards right out in front. It seems to me that that is the plain meaning of it. My hon. friend asked what the rule was-whether it was two hundred yards to the right or to the left, or whether you had to draw a line across the front of the stream, from headland to headland, as it were, and measure two hundred yards out from that. I should think that it meant two hundred yards in every direction.

My hon. friend does
not seem quite to understand the difficulty. Supposing a river flows out between two narrow sand beaches, what may be called the mouth of the river will perhaps be three hundred or four hundred yards in from the body of water into which it empties. If a person is found fishing inside of the mouth of the river, how will this section apply? There is no definition of what the mouth of a river is.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He must not fish within
two hundred yards of the mouth of the river. That is, within two hundred yards of the mouth of any tributary or of any creek or stream. I believe that is especially applicable to the Fraser river, because the salmon come up and then turn and go up the tributaries.
Mr. CARVELL * Would not that apply to any river in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I suppose it would, but
it is more especially applicable to the conditions in the Fraser river. It is thought well to keep people away from fishing within two hundred yards of the mouth of the stream, because the salmon congregate near the mouth of a river and there may be very great slaughter. It is not so much applicable to the case of a river running into the sea as it is to a creek or stream.

Then, I must ask the Department of Marine and Fisheries to pay this man, to whose case I have particular reference, his money back, because that was the very point involved in the decision against him. The river in question is the Clyburn river, which empties into the gulf of- St. Lawrence, and his man was held to be fishing within two hundred yards of the mouth of a river which empties into tidal waters. If the law did not apply to that river, or to a river of that kind, the man should be
given back his money and the nets that were taken from him.

It has been brought to
my attention by a gentleman who goes to the eastern section of Cape Breton island for the summer months for the purpose of catching salmon that the rivers in that part of the country are not properly guarded. This particular criticism is not directed at the present Government especially, because it applied in the same way during the incumbency of the past Government. People leave a lot of money in the various districts along the rivers where the salmon are caught by angling. These rivers will never be properly protected until you pay the guardians a decent living wage. It is ridiculous to think that men employed from June to October at twelve and a half dollars a month, or about fifty-six dollars a year, will render proper service to prevent these rivers from being poached at night.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite
right. Unless you pay men properly you cannot expect good service, and I have been struggling with the question of getting a reorganization of the whole fishery protection service on the lakes and rivers. I trust that next season the system will be ,so reorganized as to give better results. Some of these guardians are paid only twenty dollars a year, and unless a man is a great enthusiast he is not going to give much service for that.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll) had in view the Mar-garee river, when he spoke of fishery protection, and while I do not wish to particularize I can tell the minister that he has appointed as guardian one poor man who is unable to get out of the house because of rheumatism.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is his name?
The minister can find that out from, his officers. A review of most of the appointmen'.s made by the Government in that part of the country *would not hurt the service in any way.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) complained that a man without any legs at all has been removed from the office of fishery overseer.
The poor man I refer to would probably be better off if he had no legs at all, because they are an incumbrance to him now.

I am glad to hear the minister is considering the Teorgani-zaton of the fishery guardians. I am afraid, however, that a Tittle more salary will not make much difference in the result.
Mr. HAZEN; I think we should have fewer guardians) and pay them better salaries.

That is exactly it. If you had fewer officers, with jurisdiction over larger areas, these officers would not be so well known to their neighbours who engage in illegal fishing. You would get far better results if you paid your men good salaries, because they would not be afraid, or ashamed, or look upon it as a dishonourable thing to compel their neighbours to observe the law. We want, so to speak, men as guardians who do not have any neighbours; I think the minister catches my meaning.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do. Would the hon.
gentleman favour the idea that fishery guardians should be appointed entirely from outside the districts and neighbourhoods over which they have jurisdiction?

I would go a long way in that direction; you should have men who are not well known in the district.

The hon. member representing the Yukon is here. It would be .interesting for the rest of us to have some particulars as to the Government of the Yukon territory at the present time. We all know that the court staff and the staff in general have been somewhat reduced.

I shall be very glad indeed to respond to the wish expressed 'by the hon. gentleman. We have in the Yukon to-day a very complete system of government, which was cast by the Government of the distinguished gentleman who leads the Opposition in this House, in 1896 or 1897. The governmental institutions of the Yukon territory have evolved, as they have in any other new country, and they suit our conditions very well. The Government of the territory is presided over by a commissioner
18.34

who represents the federal Government in practically all its functions. Assisting him in directing local affairs is a council of ten men, representing five districts, elected from among the people, for three years. This council is known as the Yukon Council. It elects its owrn speaker, passes ordinances for the good government of the Yukon territory, and passes also upon the estimates submitted to it annually by the commissioner in a budget which is prepared by his controller for that purpose. This budget covers the expenses necessary for ^ roads, bridges, hospitals and all other incidentals in connection with the internal government of the territory. Under the commissioner of the territory is the gold commissioner, who presides over a staff of clerks, and who himself administers in a very large degree the Yukon Placer Act, under which the Yukon placer mines come. The commissioner of the territory is analogous in his pow'ers to the lieutenant governor of a province, although in some respects he has more power and in others less. The gold commissioner is a very important official, with great powers in administering the Act. Under him is a staff of clerks who look after the placer mines, the quartz mines, the coal mines and the timber. I need not observe that the policing of the territory is done by the Royal Northwest Mounted Police under the direction of a commandant located in Dawson, with another station at Whitehorse in the southern end of the territory.
The items which go to make up this $128,000, the $215,000 and the $100,000, a total of 353,000, arc the usual items required for the government of the territory, for the repairs, upkeep and making of new roads and trails, for our rivers, for the care of our sick, and for the general expenses of the Yukon territory.
I might say, in passing, that the prospects of the territory are brighter than they have been for sofne time. I regret to observe that there are some doubting Thomases, but facts are facts. While a few years ago the revenues of the territory had somewhat declined and the gold output has declined very considerably, to-day,
I am glad to inform the House, the gold output is increasing. In 1912 we produced about $5,500,000, and in 1913 a little over $6,000,000. We have to-day very nearly $25,000,000 of real money invested in dredging and hydraulic works in the Yukon territory.
Has the mail service between the other parts of Canada and the Yukon territory been improved?

Very much improved. For many years the people in the territory were penalized on account of the extra cost of money orders. As my hon. friend from Rouville knows, we had to pay double rates, but now the same rate prevails in the Yukon for money orders as in the rest of Canada. Our mail is carried in the winter as well as in the summer, just as in the rest of Canada. For many years there were certain restrictions. We could not get heavy articles, only certain classes of mail, in the winter time. Now the post office will accept for the Yukon anything that it accepts for any other portion of Canada. The provisions of parcel post have been extended to the territory.
What about the gold dust ? When I was Postmaster General, a petition was sent by the miners asking that gold dust be sent by mail at the usual rate.
The great proportion of our gold dust is shipped by mail. It is not shipped as dust, but the dust is melted into bricks and the bricks are sent in small canvass bags, which, of course, are insured.
Gold bricks.
Real gold bricks.

The minister might give us the names of the officials and the salaries they receive, also a brief synopsis of what the local council does with this money. Is there any probability of the Yukon territory becoming part of British Columbia ? In my recent reading, I think I have seen some discussion on that question. I am not sure, but I understand that there is a feeling in British Columbia against including the Yukon territory in that province; perhaps the same feeling extends to the Yukon as well. I should like to know whether any correspondence or negotiations have been had in regard to this matter. Has the Yukon Council or the British Columbia Government made any suggestions along this line ?

So far as the Department of the Interior is concerned, I can say authoritatively that we have had no communications either with the British Columbia Government or with the Yukon council in reference to the annexing of Yukon
territory to the province of British Columbia. I would not say positively that there has been xio correspondence with any department of the Government on the subject, but there has been none to my knowledge. I saw the despatch to which the hon. gentleman refers, which was to the effect that at a meeting recently held in the Yukon a protest was made against a rumour that had gone abroad that the Yukon was about to be annexed to the province of British Columbia. I have not heard any expression of feeling, directly or indirectly, so far as British Columbia is concerned. It is a very large question, of course, and no application having been
made to the department, I would not dare to express an opinion as to the prospects of that being brought about in the near future. I may say that we have not the details of the disposition of the $125,000 which we allow as a grant to the Yukon council; these are published in the form of an annual report made each year by the council.
