Dominion Lands and Parks-Salaries of the Outside Service, $465,000.
Of what does the Outside Service consist?

The above sum is required to pay the salaries of agents and clerks in Dominion Lands offices, crown timber agencies in the West; also sub-agents, timber inspectors, forest rangers, homestead inspectors, etc. According to a statement prepared on the 31st of October, 1913, there were 441 officials employed in the Dominion Lands Outside Service. The sum of $419,758 is necessary to pay their salaries, and the balance, $45,242, is required to provide for increases in salaries and for new appointments when needed in the ensuing year.

How many new officials does my hon. friend intend to appoint? Is it true that the minister allows officials to take part in provincial elections, say in Alberta or in Saskatchewan, or in Dominion elections? It has been rumoured time and again that a great many of these officials get very busy at election time. I have heard of some of them almost getting into trouble for it. Does my hon. friend take very strong ground on that? If he finds any official taking part in elections, even provincial elections, does he do what the Minister of Customs says he would aspire to do although I am afraid he never does it warn them that they must not take part in these elections? I can understand that a warning might be quite futile if not followed up by action. Men in these positions have naturally very great power over the people, in a new part of the country particularly, and I think it is very essential that they should attend to their own business and not to the'business of any political party, I do not care to what party they belong.

It is not the intention to appoint any new officials to our present

staff except where we consider it absolutely necessary. We have not in contemplation at present the appointment of any new officials. In regard to the matter of our officials taking part in elections, human nature is human nature, and I presume that the mere fact of a person being a Conservative official does not make him superior to a Liberal official, and I think there is a tendency for an official, no matter what his position may be, to favour the party in power. Personally I am not at all in favour of Dominion Government officials participating in elections, provincial or Dominion. I have heard charges made in this House which when followed up I found were not based upon facts. I have not had conveyed to me the fact that any officials of this department have, since I have been in the department, participated in any elections, Dominion or provincial. Most assuredly I am not in favour of our officials participating actively in elections. I have not yet had occasion to warn any of them except in the communications I have had with those against whom charges have been made upon the floor of Parliament, which were denied by these gentlemen. I am sure that the hon. gentleman took that stand when he was on this side of the House and followed it out, no doubt, to the utmost of his power. I shall endeavour to do the same.
Has the minister warned his officials in any general way as to what action would follow participation in any election ?
We never judge any person guilty until he is at least accused.
Is the department's policy of a nature that will prevent these men taking part in elections ?
If there were an election coming on in the near future I think I would feel it my duty to warn, publicly and generally, the officials not to participate in elections.

I would recall a glaring case in the constituency of Edmonton during the late provincial elections. A homestead inspector in the Peace river district, who was not appointed by my hon. friend, but under the late Administration, took on himself to conie out publicly and take part in the provincial contest. He addressed several meetings publicly and did everything in his power to have the Conservative candidate in that constituency elected. That is public
property, it was published in the newspapers at the time, and I think reference has also been made to it in this House.
I am not aware that the minister has ever taken any public stand in regard to the participation of his officials in elections, whether provincial or Dominion. I know that under the policy of the late Administration no official of the Department of the Interior could take part in a provincial or a Dominion election. If an official disobeyed the instructions to that effect, he did so at the peril of his office. Is the present Minister of the Interior prepared to take that stand ?

If there were an election in sight, I think I would consider it my duty to warn the officials of my department not to take an active part in it. Such a warning may have been sent out by my predecessor, and sent out in good faith, but the hon. member knows quite well that a good deal of latitude is allowed, and the officials to my personal knowledge do not follow these instructions.
They disobey them?
Certainly.

Is the minister prepared to punish these men? If he desires,
I will give him the name of the inspector I refer to-Joshua Fletcher, a homestead inspector of the Peace River district. I have it in black and white. Mr. Fletcher addressed a letter to me in which he stated his reasons for supporting the Conservative candidate. There is no question at all that this man took part in the provincial election. This is rather a glaring ease of partisanship, and I think the committee is entitled to some statement from the minister as to what he would do in a case of that kind. I am prepared to make the assertion that this man took part in an election in a partisan way.
When was it?

In the provincial
election in Alberta last year.
I do not think charges have been made against Mr. Fletcher; at least, I have no note of any.

I think the statement has been previously made on the floor of this House that Mr. Fletcher participated in the Alberta provincial election. I am not so anxious to get after this man as to know what the policy of the Government
is in regard to this matter. Another case came under my observation. Shortly after the change of Government in 1911 a homestead inspector in the district of Wetaski-win took part in an election. He left his work, put another man in his.place, and participated in a provincial election for something over two weeks, and yet nothing has been done by the department, as I understand. The man was allowed to draw his money, although he went on the stump and solicited votes for his candidate.
I am bringing these cases to the attention of the minister merely to know what .he . would do should a similar case arise.

I remember now that the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) brought Mr. Fletcher's case to my attention. I have communicated with that gentleman and sent him a copy of 'Hansard,' but I have not heard from him yet.

I was surprised to hear the minister say that no case of a homestead inspector taking part in an election had been brought to his attention. If the minister will look up the records in his own department, he will find that a homestead inspector _ resigned on the first of April, ivent campaigning for two weeks, was put up as a candidate on the 17th of the month, was defeated, and was reappointed to his old position at the beginning of the next month. The minister must know that that man was reappointed. I refer to Ambrose Grey, a man who, I think, had no right to the position in the first place who had been convicted of breaking the law, and who, report says, had never been known to earn an honest living in his life till he took the position with the Government. That the minister reappointed him is not so bad as to put him in the same district where he ran as candidate. I have had several letters from homesteaders complaining that whenever there was a dispute they got a little the worst of it, because they did not support the inspector at the last election. I do not think the minister or any member of the Government can hand this-back and say, you did the same. I de:y them to produce any case under the previous Government of a man being a political candidate, failing as such, and then being allowed to go back to his old position. It is true that some men who were homestead inspectors at one time now represent constituencies in the provincial legis-

latures but they resigned a year or perhaps two years before they ran as candidates. I would like to Tecall one case to the minister, that of a man named Harry Bow-tell. The man claimed that his name had been put up at the party nomination without his knowledge. It came to the ears of the late Minister of the Interior. He would take no excuse, but dismissed the man from office. Is it the policy of the present minister to appoint a man, get him well acquainted with his district, train him for a candidate, let him be put up at an election, and then, if he fails, give him back his old position?

The hon, member has
brought forward a case that I have no personal cognizance of. I do not know when that homestead inspector resigned.
On the first of April, 1913; he was reappointed on the 1st of May, and the election was on the 17th of April.

As the hon. member says, it might be difficult to cite a parallel case. I do not wish to hark back to find an excuse, but I think a parallel case occurred in- my own constituency. What brought it more forcibly to my mind was that in this particular instance my opponent was a homestead inspector who resigned after he received his nomination. It is true, he was not reappointed in that district, but a gentleman of the name of Thomas Young, who was a homestead inspector in the Dauphin district, and who did not resign until a long time after his nomination, was reappointed to his position after the general election in which he was defeated.
You can never excuse that kind of thing.
No, I am not quoting it as an excuse.
Was the gentleman put back in the district where he was a candidate?
That is my recollection.

I have been getting a great deal of correspondence on this subject. People are complaining and justly so. You can understand that if certain people had worked and voted against a man in an election, if a dispute arose about land and there were two contestants for that land, one of whom was a supporter of the homestead inspector and the other a supporter 
of his opponent, the latter would naturally get the worst of it. I would like the minister to look into this matter, and if he finds that I am correct in this statement, I think it is only fair that he should remove this main from the district. If the department simply cannot get along without the services of this gentleman, they should iat least take him away from the district where he was a candidate and where he suffered defeat.

This is a somewhat
serious case. I am glad that the minister does not make the excuse that somebody else -did it. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is not here, but I will call his attention to the remarks of -my hon. friend when he -comes in. If I understand the situation aright, this man- is an inspector. He gets acquainted with the people, of course. He resigns his position in April and becomes a candidate. He is defeated on the 1st of May, and he is reappointed amongst the very people whose votes he was soliciting a week before. It might not be so serious under some other conditions, but the seriousness of the matter in this case is that the men whose votes he was soliciting knew that, with the prospect of another election coming on, the decision as to whether they would get the patents for their lands depended on him. Giving a man the power to bribe, threaten or frighten people in this way is, I think, without excuse under any conditions whatever.
I cannot believe that the Minister of the Interior, with his usual fairness in dealing with these matters, has had this circumstance brought to his attention in this way before. It places the men who are looking for the patents for their land in the position that it is possible that they will be discriminated against if they do not agree in the future to support this gentleman if he wants to be a 'Candidate, or if they -have not supported him in the past. With respect to an ordinary official of the Customs, or some other department, it would be an improper thing to do, but it would not have nearly the same consequences if he were appointed under similar conditions as those which would attend the Teappointment of an office holder of this kind. I understand that this gentleman was in trouble at one time himself; but I am not going to dwell upon that because we are all more or less human. Any of us may get into trouble at some time in our lives. The seriousness of this matter is that this man has been reappointed where he has been a candidate
and where he may be a candidate again, placing in his power the people with whom he-is dealing officially, and whose support he may solicit again.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not want to indulge in the tu quoque argument that we have been hearing iso much about, but I would like to call the attention of my hon. friend, who is so much shocked by this transaction, to a certain transaction in the province of New Brunswick. In 1899 I was a candidate for the House of Assembly in Sunbury, and the gentleman who opposed me was a gentleman of the name of Harrison. Soon after the election Mr. Harrison was appointed inspector of fisheries for the district. Another election came on in 1903, where I was again a candidate, and Mr. Harrison resigned his position as inspector of fisheries, again ran in the election, and two weeks after the election was reappointed to the same office. I may tell my hon. friend that this transaction occurred under a government of which he was a member.
But we are not accustomed to that sort of thing in the West.

I rather answered my
hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) before he made his remarks: I said that the conditions would not be the same with any other officer.

I would like to ask the minister whether he will consider this request that I have put to him; that is, that if he finds this complaint well-founded, he will remove this man from the district in which he is now employed. That is what the people want. Everybody is complaining about it.

As I have already intimated, this is the first mention I have heard about this case. It has not been brought to my attention. While I recognize that I am responsible for everything that is done in the Interior Department, as a matter of fact, I was absent when this occurred. I have not received any protests or complaints against this Government in the line indicated by the hon. gentleman. None oi those homesteaders has sent in any complaints to the department; if so, they have not been brought to my attention, and certainly if they do, the official will have to account for anything that he may do, because I will thoroughly investigate the matter.

They surely would not
get their patents if they complained against him.

Yes, they know that there is a very fair man at the head of the Interior Department. I would not allow the matter to go by default if accusations of that nature were made against any official of the department.

I will not charge the minister with having any knowledge of this matter, but I have received several letters and complaints with regard to it. If the minister states that in the event of complaints being made to him he will remove this officer from that district, I will refer these complaints to him.
I will investigate the complaints before removing him.

I think we have a right to some statement of policy from the minister. Many charges have been brought to the attention of the minister of people not only indulging in politics, but of having been guilty of criminal offences and still being retained in the employ of the department. Last year I had a question -on the Order Paper in regard to J. K. Smith of Moosejaw. I asked whether he was still in the employ of the Government. The answer was in the affirmative. I asked if the minister w7as aware that he had been convicted of perjury, and the answer was in the negative. I presume that that would be sufficient notice to the minister that a charge had been made against Mr. Smith. But I am advised that he is still in the employ of the Government. I have here a statement which has been taken from the records in Regina showing that this man was convicted of perjury in 1908, three or four years before he was appointed by the present Government, and that he underwent a sentence of six months' imprisonment. Still he is appointed by the present Government. I presume that whoever recommended him must have had knowledge of this fact. Many cases of this kind have been brought to the attention of the minister, and I think that some attention should be paid to them and that we should know what his policy is in regard to retaining ex-convicts in the service of the department. We hear a good deal about the tu quoque argument; we have just heard it from the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen.)
He was only joking.

I do not know whether he was joking or not, but the cheer which he received from his followers seemed to indicate that the policy of the present Gov-

eminent and their supporters is that they shall retain in office, and that it is all right to retain in office, and put back in office, defeated candidates occupying the position that this gentleman does, because the previous Government did it. If those cheers meant anything they meant that. If those cheeTS meant anything else they were thrown away. They were an insult to the intelligence of the House if they meant anything else. I think we should know whether the policy of the Government is that they are to retain in office men who have been defeated candidate.
Tell us what you like about what the late Government did, but that is no answer. The argument of hon. gentlemen opposite, if it means anything, means that they approve of the policy of the present Government in doing such work as the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. W. H. White) claims has been done. We have a right to know from the Minister of the Interior, in the first place, whether he approves of ex-convicts being employed by his department, and, in the second place, whether he purposes retaining homestead inspectors in their positions, when they have been candidates in elections. There may be peculiar circumstances in the case of J. K. Smith, which would make it quite fair for the minister to retain him in the service, but it is high time we should have a statement of the policy of the department as to this matter.

Does not the hon.
gentleman think it would be a good idea for him, instead of asking the minister to pronounce on a suppositious case, to propound a policy for himself?
We are not in power.
I am well aware you are not in power, and I do not think there is any likelihood that you will be in power during your lifetime or mine.
Hear, hear.

When the hon. member (Air. Levi Thomson) speaks about exconvicts being retained in office, I think I am justified in asking him if he objects to that, and, if so, when he changed his mind. It is not so very long since hon. gentlemen opposite followed the policy of taking a man out of prison and rewarding him with a position at three times the salary he had before he went into prison. When we remind them of this, they accuse us of using the tu quoque

argument; but I think we have a perfect right to remind them of what they have done in the past until they give some tangible evidence that they have repented. I wish to make a few serious observations regarding the conduct of the homestead inspector in the electoral riding of Moosejaw in the last provincial election. Without fear of contradiction, I make the statement to the Minister of the Interior that since the Conservatives have taken over the administration of the Moosejaw lands, the administration of these lands has come to be a scandal. A year ago I made in this House an assertion to the minister who is now Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), to the effect that I would cite a case where a man had held a homestead and it had been taken from him and given to a Conservative for no other reason than that the man who received it was a Conservative. I could tell of cases of Conservatives who, for no other reason than they were Conservatives, had been restored to homesteads

of which they had been properly deprived. One case regarding a homestead , close to the village of Gravelbourg has already been before the House. My hon. friend: the Minister of the. Interior cannot take refuge in this case by saying that he was not Minister of the Interior then, because he was. It is the case of the Beaubien homestead. Mr. Beaubien lives in the incorporated, village of Gravelbourg. He is a butcher. He was an alleged Liberal up to the evening of the 21st day of September, 1911. He was always seeking something and knocking at the door, and he right-about-faced when the Government went out of power. He held a homestead close to the village of Gravelbourg. His family lived at Gravelbourg all the time, and any sleeping he ever did on the homestead was less than a week and was not legal residence, because it was without the presence of his wife and family. The minister knows that, if a man's business is in town, his wife and family must reside on the homestead in order that he may have legal residence there.
If he has not a, wife, what then?

My hon. friend will
have to get his information elsewhere. I am busy. The homestead was held by Mr. Beaubien for three or four years. Mr. Beaubien's rights were cancelled and another man was given entry. I forget his name; I would know it if I heard it; it is a French name also. This man had put in all his crop. Mr. Beaubien went through the countryside saying that he had a pull with the department, and that he would get this entrant put out, although he himself had not a shadow of a claim to the homestead. This new entrant put in his crop and reaped it, and then the agent of the Dominion lands at Gravelbourg, who was a friend of Beaubien's, was charged with setting fire to the crop. Without any cause, without any reason or rhyme, the department, while that crop was on the ground and not threshed, sent a wire saying that Beaubien was restored. That was on the 16th day of September, and on the same day I sent to the minister a long telegram, which I paid for out of my own pocket with my own hard-earned money; I did not send it collect. The telegram is as follows:
Moosejaw, Sask., September, 16, 1913. Minister of the Interior,
Ottawa.
Please refer, file northeast 22-11-5 west third and investigate. False reports of home-
stead inspectors and false statements of Beaubien have caused universal public indignation in the district. I am advised that department has lately reinstated Beaubien. Citizens in vicinity of Gravelbourg are in furore because of this report. The conduct of this matter : seems to constitute a disgrace and shame. Will you authorize full investigation and give me opportunity to submit evidence and call witnesses and withdraw reinstatement of Beaubien in meantime?
(Sgd) W. E. Knowles.
That telegram went to the minister. I followed it with a letter on the 17th, the next day. That same day I received a wire from the minister's office at Ottawa saying that the minister was in Winnipeg and that the telegram was being forwarded. From that day to this, in spite of my urgent telegram and letter stating that false reports and false statements ' had been made respecting the homestead, I have never had one iota or scrap of information from the hon. minister who wants to conduct such an honest department and who says that the people of the West know that there is an honest man at the head of the Department of the Interior. I have sat in this Parliament for nine sessions, and this is the only telegram I have ever sent the minister. To this telegram, informing the minister of a public scandal and asking for an investigation, I received in_ reply a wire saying that the minister was in Winnipeg, and that the matter would be placed before him on his return. From that time until this day, I have never heard a whisper about it. Does the minister think that treatment of that kind will in any way mitigate the feeling that is sweeping through the Moosejaw district, that the administration of lands in the West is not a straight, honest and nonpartisan administration? I do not say that personally the minister had anything to do with it, but whom else can we talk to about the matter? We cannot talk to
9	p.m. the homestead inspectors, every one of whom worked during the provincial elections of 1912 as if their lives depended upon the result of their efforts. It was decided to hold over the cancellation proceedings until the 1st of April, 1912.
As the hon. gentleman is aware, during the last few years a general order has been issued in November or December of each year protecting all homestead entries against cancellation until about the first of the following April. This is done for the purpose of giving a large number of poor homesteaders an opportunity of going away to engage in work to keep them during the winter, without running the risk of having their entries cancelled during their absence. (Reading):

Investigation delayed on account of the court case.
The delay was on account of the court case to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I was in the West when the hon. gentleman's telegram was received. He was protected until
April, 1913; he was instructed that he would have to be upon his homestead on the first day of that month. It was during his absence in Winnipeg with his wife, because of this operation, that the gentleman was unable to comply with the departmental instructions and, he, having submitted evidence to that effect which was backed up toy other evidence, it was only humane, I think, on the part of the officers in the department to reinstate him, and not cancel his entry, especially in view of the fact that he had 180 acres under crop. It would have been a serious matter to have taken his farm from him when he had given evidence of good faith, undertaken cultivation to this extent, and especially when advantage was taken of his absence in Winnipeg; and the department considered it only right and proper and what any minister or official should do under the circumstances to reinstate him in his entry. I do not see anything about that which should raise a whirlwind of indignation in my hon. friend's constituency. I think he is endeavouring to make a mountain out of a molehill when he tries to show that there was something crooked or dishonest, something that would not stand the light of day, in that transaction. The file is open to inspection, the papers will be brought down in a few days, and everything I have stated will be found to be 'borne out by the file. [DOT]

My hon. friend knows that I did not intend any charge against him other than that he did not give personal attention to these matters. The case is one of the most dirty political cases I have ever known. Beaubien has had the place for six years and has never done a week's residence on it. His entry had been cancelled, rightly cancelled, the homestead taken away from him, and in April, 1912, he was told to get his defence in. By some hook or crook between the officers and homestead inspectors, they let the matter drift on for over a year, and then they were compelled to move, and they" cancelled his entry. Then hn comes in with a cock-and-bull story about being in Winnipeg. The minister has entirely the advantage of me, because he has the papers before him and I have never seen the file; but he has not said a word about a single bit of residence duty that this man has (done in six years; I can tell of Grits in good standing whose entries his department has cancelled; tout because this gentle-
man was a Tory, he has been protected out of all reason. He is a man who does the low kind of work that is required sometimes. That fellow, the tool of the Tory party, has sot such favours and concessions that my hon. friend, if he knew the ins and outs of them, would beashamed of hisde-partment. The hon. minister says that the homestead inspector says this and that. That is what I am complaining of; the homestead inspectors make false reports, as I said in my telegram. In that telegram I asked:
Will you authorize full investigation and give me opportunity to submit evidence?
He says that he sent Mr. Cuttle there, but he never told me a word about it. I do not accuse him of any discourtesy, but he did not give a rap whether I heard of it or not, he was so busy with other things. If the minister has not officials whom he can trust to do things right, he ought to do them himself, and the only circumstance under which he could ignore a telegram of this kind would be when he had officials around him who could be trusted to deal with such matters courteously and fairly. He has not such officials in his homestead inspectors and some others, and he cannot say a word about one day's honest homestead duty that this man ever did. I wish to say a word about these homestead inspectors. I have here the sworn diaries of a few of them during the provincial elections, and they certainly were busy boys.
I have here the diary of a homestead inspector named W. H. Erratt, a brother or nephew of the man from whom my hon. friend bought the site for the examining warehouse in Moosejaw, Mr. J. It is wonderful how many of these boys hang around the town at * H.Q.' at election times, in the committee rooms and thereabouts at ' H.Q.' The fact is, he was 117
working in the elections. He was a Moose-jaw man. He was not out looking after the homesteaders, but he was attending to political matters in that town. During those seven precious days he made no inspections. Let us take his diary from June 29 to July 17, nineteen days. He made two inspections and took two applications. Mr. Smyth, of Swift Current, appeared for Shields and objected to the jurisdiction of the court on the ground that Anderson, J.P., was secretary of the Liberal Association, and that Graham was returning officer appointed by the Liberal Government, and that they were both active party politicians. The solicitor representing the Attorney General's Department stated that the prosecution was not ready to proceed and asked for an adjournment. Mr. Smyth pointed out that the whole case was an election dodge for the purpose of throwing discredit on the Conservative party and influencing votes. The justices of the peace decided to adjourn the matter to Regina to be tried by Magistrate Trant there, and although Shields had been admitted to bail by the order of Judge Johnson of the Supreme Court, who had characterized the proceedings as preposterous and unworthy even of Russia, the magistrates again, at the request of the solicitor representing the Attorney General, absolutely refused bail in any amount. Shields was for the second time taken on the train to Regina and subjected to the same indignities en route. He remained in Regina jail until the 10th of July before an order for bail could be procured-the police

magistrate at Regina granting the order after his previous experience with Judge Johnson. The police magistrate remanded the case until the 17th of July.
So determined were the Liberals to keep Mr. Shields locked up without any cause, that when he was passing out of the police court after having furnished bail on this occasion, three or four heelers made an attempt to arrest him again, although he had already been bailed twice. This was persecution which the public would stand for no longer, and Mr. Shield's friends insisted on seeing a warrant, which the parties to the arrest could not produce. Mr. Shield's friends threw the special constable aside and rescued him from their illegal custody and took him away where he would avoid any further humiliation.
Thus it was that the good citizens of Saskatchewan had to uphold law, and order, and British justice in that province by bodily force.
On the 17th of July Shields again appeared in pursuance to the remand before the police magistrate at Regina, going all the way from Swift Current for that purpose. No evidence was offered by the prosecution whatever and no witnesses were produced, so the case was dismissed. Attached hereto is exhibit ' C,' a copy of the certificate of dismissal.

He there got acquainted with the land agent, Mr. Oliver, and Mr. Oliver gave him a letter of introduction to Mr. Smyth, the homestead inspector. Thereafter, during the term of their joint liberty, Marsh Jackson and Smyth paraded around the constituency of Wadena holding meetings, in secret largely, and attempting to intimidate the Galicians and other foreign voters in the constituency until ultimately Jackson was arrested and a little later Smyth was arrested. That is the history of these two gentlemen. Jackson came to the constituency, wearing, on the inside of his coat lapel, a badge on which was inscribed ' Chief of the Dominion Secret Service.' That badge is still in the possession of the provincial authorities at Regina. Mr. Jackson not only carried a badge, but he carried personal cards on which was inscribed the very same thing. If the minister wants to look up the record of this pet friend of his, he can go down to the Commissioner of Police and ask Colonel Sherwood what he knows about him, because a sample of one of these cards was sent to Colonel Sherwood, and he wrote back saying that Jackson had never. had anything to do with the Secret Service of the Dominion of Canada. But
everybody knows that Jackson is the handy man of the Minister of Public Works in the city of Winnipeg, everybody knew who sent him to Saskatchewan, and everybody likewise knew that when Jackson arrived the first person that he looked up was the Dominion Lands agent. Why did he look up the Domioion Lands agent? He was introduced by the Dominion Lands agent to the homestead inspector for the Humboldt district, and, following that introduction, these two gentlemen, Mr. Marsh Jackson with his badge, ' Chief of the Secret Service of Canada,' and Mr. Smyth, went around holding meetings among the foreigners with a young Galician girl to act as interpreter. They told a number of Galicians that the Conservative Government were going to take certain vacant railway lands in the district away from the railways and give them to settlers if they would only vote right. These Galicians, being far-sighted people along practical lines, said, ' We had better get these lands before the election,' and one day twenty-five of them started upon a pilgrimage to the land office at Humboldt. Mr. Smyth had to go and head them off and tell them that they would have to wait until the election was over. This was the sort of work that Smyth and Jackson were doing. Jackson, as well as Smyth, was taken to Regina. Jackson was released. The Minister of Public Works knows why Jackson was released; he was released because he turned King's evidence, and gave the authorities at Regina a list of the official and other political agents who had been sent out from Manitoba, by my hon. friend knows whom, to different parts of Saskatchewan to work in that election. With regard to the other charge 1 think it is the most cruel, cowardly display of vicious meanness that I ever heard of. I was then approached by one Gaetz who claimed to be Deputy Chief of Police of the province of Saskatchewan, who made the following suggestion: that if I would sign an affidavit to the effect that I had received instructions directly or indirectly and also money with which to bribe electors from the Hon. Robert Rogers, then Minister of the Interior, I would be allowed to go and no charges preferred against me. Mr. Calder and Mr. Anderson of the Attorney General's department, after which Gaetz again approached me and again suggested that the easiest way out of my trouble was to sign an affidavit which contained charges against the Hon. Robert Rogers. I refused to do as he requested and he then took me to the Mounted Police office where 1 was placed in a steel cage, such as is used for the most desperate criminals. The next morning I was taken before Magistrate Trant, who remanded the case for a week, in the meantime, provincial constables were scouring the country trying to get evidence to substantiate the charge that I was arrested on, which they failed to do, and when I came up for trial the charge on which I was arrested was dropped entirely. I was then told that they had another charge against me, that of telling a Galician not to vote.
Regarding this second charge the facts are as follows: I was making inspections in a Galician settlement, and about six o'clock one evening I drove to a house and asked to stay over night. I stayed there over night but did not discuss politics in any way. The next morning the daughter of this farmer, who, although a Galician girl, spoke good English, asked me which way I was going. I informed her that I was going north and she asked permission to ride two miles to a neighbour's whose place I was passing. When we had driven a mile on the way we met two Galicians on foot. The girl asked me to stop, as she wished to speak to her countrymen, and a short conversation took place in the Galician language. I had no idea what was being said but the conversation did not last a minute. A mile further on the girl got out of the rig at the neighbour's she was going to, and I drove on to make my inspections. The two Galicians we met were entire strangers to. me. I had never seen them before and I did not see them again until this second charge was brought against me when I came up for my hearing at Regina. They were given money and taken up there to swear that the Galician girl had told them

If he had read an affidavit of the Erime Minister of Great Britain and it turned out to be false he would have done an injury for which he owed reparation, but there is a wide margin between a poor half-breed and the Prime Minister of Britain, and this was a half-breed that he did not know at all. The hon. gentleman says that Mr. Glen Campbell has not gone far enough and that he ought to prosecute. Five minutes ago he said that this half-breed had perjured himself. He has it in his power to prosecute him and lay an information against this half-breed. Will he do it? It is in his power; the Scott Government is in power.
Order.

The hon. member for
Moosejaw would like to do that, would he?
What is the question?

The hon. gentleman
seems to object to my asking the hon. member for Humboldt to lay an information. Perhaps he wants to do it himself?

You misrepresent me.
The hon. member for Humboldt asked you if you did not have a justification for what he had done, and now you are going on to say what he should do in the future, which is a different thing altogether. Why do you not answer the question and sit down?

The hon. gentleman's
justification is not a good one.
That is what you say, but you have not shown that to be the case.

I have shown it several times and he has admitted it. His justification has fallen to the ground. Nothing but the truth of the case would have justified it. Now he wants Mr. Glen Campbell to prosecute the half-breed who, on his knees, bended before the hon. member for Humboldt and asked for alms; the half-breed who could not keep his family; who had his foot frozen off a while ago-now only nipped-this is the halfbreed that the hon. gentleman thinks Mr. Glen Campbell should prosecute. The hon. gentleman's friends are in power in Sas-
136ft
katchewan. The provincial Government alone have the administration of the Criminal Code. The prosecution of the halfbreed is under the control of the Scott Government of Saskatchewan. The hon. gentleman can assist them by producing the affidavits and by saying what he has said in the House, that he does not believe [DOT] it is true, that he believes Mr. Glen Campbell instead. If he does that he will be rendering material aid. I do not think he has the slightest intention of carrying out that promise any more than he has of carrying out his promise to apologize. But perhaps the events of the evening will at least show him that he must be more careful and that he is not justified in reading the affidavit of a man he does not know, whether he be a half-breed or not, and whom he has no special reason to believe, when he admits the contents of that am-davit seriously damaged the reputation of a man whom he was bound to have held to he an honourable man.

AVe certainly have had a lesson to-night on our responsibility as members of this House; we have been taught by the Solicitor General in good set terms that employees of this Government must not be challenged by members on this side of the House, no matter what their offence may be, or how solemnly the accusation may have been made against them.
I did not say that.
My hon. friend did not say that, but that was the logical sequence of his argument.
Permit me to say-
If the Solicitor General, who is good at interrupting, will be good enough to take back the suggestion he made, we will understand where we are.
I have made-
In the meantime, will he be good enough to permit me to proceed with my remarks ?
I rise to a point of order.
I have the floor. I ask your protection, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Meighen) rises to a point of order.

The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Oliver) ascribes to me the statement that the conduct of a Government official is not to be challenged no matter what a
the charge against him may be; I made no such statement.
There is no point of order in that.
Does the hon. gentleman say that he can ascribe to me language I never used, and then contend that I cannot rise to a point of order to contradict it ?
I did not say the hon. gentleman made that statement. ,
Oh, all right, then.

The Solicitor General did not take his point of order well. I said that we had understood from his remarks that we had received a lesson on this side of the House as to what our conduct must be towards the high and mighty officials of this Government; that we must not challenge their conduct, no matter what they do, nor upon what_ authority we have warrant for challenging their conduct. I want to say to the Solicitor General and to the members of the Government, that in my humble judgment, when an affidavit making a serious charge against an official of this Government is placed in the hands of a member of the Opposition, that member of the Opposition is doing much less than his duty if he does not bring to the attention of the Government in parliamentary form, the charge that has been made under affidavit. AVho is the Solicitor General, who declares so roundly and so loudly against charges being made against officials of this Government, even on affidavit ? He is the colleague of the Minister of the Interior, who to-night read, not an affidavit, but a letter from a convicted criminal, making a charge against my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely), a scoundrelly charge, which he dare not make under any other circumstance. What has the Solicitor General to say to that ?
Will the hon. gentleman tell me what crime this man was convicted of ?
Yes, I will. He was convicted of the crime of intimidation in an election. He was punished for that crime, and he deserved his punishment.
Will the hon. gentleman show me in the Criminal Code where that is made a crime?

My hon. friend may have dictionary meaning, which does not cor-

respond with the word I used, but I take the ordinary commonsense meaning, that a man who pays a fine of $50 has been convicted of a crime. The Solicitor General may call it an offence instead of a crime; I care not what he calls it; the point is, that an official of this Government infringed the laws of this country, and was punished for doing it, and to-night he has been upheld in so doing by a responsible minister, and by the party on that side of the House.
And then he read a dirty slander in a letter.

And in defence of this man, the Minister of the Interior makes himself a party to this scoundrelly slander, not against an ex-member of this House, but against a member, sitting in his place in the House. I claim, Mr. Chairman, that the members on this side of the House are entitled to protection at your hands, and that they have not received it to-night. And if we do not get protection from the Chair, I want to say that we are not like people who cannot protect ourselves.
The hon. member has no right to attack the Chair in that manner. When both sides are going too far, it is very hard for the Chairman to interfere, unless he is called upon to do so.
I called ' Order ' when the hon. member was reading that slanderous, cowardly statement, and I think he should have been stopped.

I do not want to detract from the dignity of your office, Mr. Chairman, or to find fault with your conduct, because I think your intention is to discharge the duties of your responsible position with due consideration; but I have stated the position as it has appeared to me. I want to say that the minister, in my hearing to-night, gave to the House the reason why Smyth was appointed, and the reason was because he had been an active partisan against the member for Humboldt. The evidence is, in this and other cases, that when this Government came to power, one of their first acts was to discharge practically en masse the land officials in the employ of the late Government, and to appoint in their places avowed, well-recognized political partisans, for the purpose of doing exactly what Smyth was fined for doing, that is, paralyzing the franchise of the homesteaders of the prairie West, depriving them of their right to vote

as their consciences dictated, or depriving them of their homesteads in the alterna" tive. I have said before, and I repeat tonight, that that policy and that action on the part of the Government of the day has had more than a little to do with the shrinkage of homestead entries that has taken place since the Government has attained office.
I have not been in the House during the whole of this discussion, and the cases to which I will allude may possibly have been already discussed. In the Peace River country, in the Grand Prairie district, where at the time of the last provincial elections not more than half a dozen homestead patents had been received, but where there were hundreds of settlers, the homestead inspector took the platform on behalf of the local Conservative candidate, and declared to the people in good set terms the necessity under which they were of supporting the local Conservative candidate, because he was a supporter of this Dominion Government, for whom Mr. Fletcher was working. Mr. Fletcher had been appointed by myself as Minister of the Interior. I verily believe that he did as he did on that occasion under stress and threat from this Government that if he did not get out and hustle for the Conservative candidate in that election he would lose his position. Put yourself in the position of those homestead settlers on the prairie, 350 miles from railroad communication-men who have put their money, their time and their energy into their homesteads-and up against the proposition that they Shall vote Tory or shall take chances on losing their homestead, and you must admit that we have not a free country or an administration that ought to have the support of the people of Canada. You cannot have proper encouragement to settlement under those cir-(cumstances. That is not an isolated ease. One of these political partisans, a man who spent his life in party politics, was appointed a homestead inspector, not in my constituency but immediately across the line in the adjoining constituency, a man whose business at elections was to take care of the half-breed vote. A provincial election came along and Mr. Ambroise Grey was the Conservative candidate. He is also the man who has the say as to whether a homesteader is to get his patent or not, as to whether a dispute is to be decided in favour of this or that man. Is that a fair deal to the homestead electors in that district? Mr. Ambroise Grey was defeated. I asked the question whether he was a home-
1S67
stead inspector or not, and I was told that he had resigned. As soon as the election was over, he was back again as homestead inspector. Just before I came down to Parliament, this same Mr. Grey and a Mr. Frank Fane, who is also in the employ of this Government, accompanied by a Mr. H.
A Mackie, a lawyer, and an ex-detective named Hoyle, were travelling in the district of Beaver river in an automobile, in order to secure evidence against the successful candidate in- the provincial election. Give this man Grey the authority of homestead inspector; give him the prestige that attaches to that position, and send him out looking for information against the elected candidate, and he surely is in a good position to secure such information. Again, it is a case of the homesteader's time, his money, his energy, everything that he has, on the one side, or support of the Tory party in the provincial legislature on the other. Such a condition never before existed in Canada; it is detrimental to the welfare of the country; it is discreditable to the Government of the day. It is true that they have not won out on it so far. I do not think they will win out on it; I think they will find that they will lose out on it; because they have already aroused an antagonism amongst the fair-minded people of the country that they will feel the force of, whenever the opportunity comes at the polls. But the point is that they have done it, and they have dared to attempt to justify it in this House, and they have been supported by their supporters in that attempt.

I do not rise for the purpose of delaying the Estimates. I would like to bring one matter to the attention of the minister. At a convention held at Emerson a short time ago, Dr. McFadden was nominated as the Conservative candidate, I understand, against the will of the people. Whether that is the case or not, I do not know and do not care. In the report of the convention, I noticed that a fight took place in which a gentleman of the name of J. E. Canham took part, who by the way is a Canadian Northern railway agent and also sub-land agent at Sprague. I bring this to the attention of the minister as a case of a Government official interfering in politics. Mr. Canham has a great deal of homestead land in his district. I am also informed,-and I believe that it is true,- that the same Mr. J. E. Canham, since becoming sub-land agent, has received patent of n.w. j 12-1-4, east of the first, on which he has never lived an hour
or done one day's work in homesteading. That is contrary to the regulations. The gentleman who gave the information I know well, and he has lived in that district for a great many years. Mr. Canham is using as campaign stuff, so to speak, that if you are a Conservative you can get patents through very easily; you do not have to put in any residence or do any homestead duties. I think it is the duty of the minister to investigate this matter. So far as Mr. J. E. Canham's taking part in an election is concerned, I do not ask the minister even to reprimand him. If I am again a candidate in the county of Provencher and Mr. Canham interferes in his official capacity, I will slap his face. In the meantime the other matter is more serious. Has Mr. J. E. Canham received patent on n.w. r section 12-1-4 wit'hout putting in any residence or homestead duties ? That is the matter which I Would like the minister to investigate.
The hon. member for Provencher knows quite well that I cannot answer him offhand, but I will make inquiries.

It is on this item thatjustly and fairly I would be able to discuss what I want to discuss, that is, the number of appointments made in the outside service of the Department of the Interior in the last year or two. The return I asked for would give me the necessary information to discuss intelligently this question, and I have not that return. This is the first item, and I presume the minister wants to get on with his programme; but if this item passes, I would like to know if the minister would consent, on the next item, after I get the return that I hope will be brought down very shortly, I *trust before he goes into Supply again, that I shall have the opportunity of discussing the increase in the number of appointments in the outside service.
I am quite agreeable that the hon. member should discuss what he desires to discuss on any item.

Will the minister assure
me that that return will be brought down before he goes again into Supply, so that I can make use of it?
Yes.

Can the hon. minister
give me any information in regard to the homestead inspectors of whom I spoke?

How could it be that in a period of nineteen days there would be only fourteen inspections made and no trouble about the matter? What business has a man to ride around in an automobiie? Why should he be at headquarters for ten days running? How did all these matters escape detection in the department at the hands of those whose duty I presume it is to check these men up?-because there is no doubt some such system.

The hon. member for Moosejaw probably is not aware of the fact that theise diaries are not kept in the department; they are filed in the local offices. The inspections are checked up by the Dominion lands agent of the district in which the homestead inspector makes his inspections. It is true that at times the inspectors spend a few days at the head office making up reports. The diaries are only sent to the department here on special occasions.
Does the minister say that he has no information in his department as to the inspections made by each homestead inspector?
No, I did not say that.
What about the case in which there were only four inspections in nineteen days? Why were those inspections not checked up?

I can quite readily understand that. The hon. gentleman knows that there are districts adjacent to Moose-jaw in which no inspections may be made, but inspections may be necessary in districts ninety miles from Moosejaw, and it takes quite a while to cover that ground. The hon. gentleman pointed out that a certain official travelled in a Conservative automobile, as he called it, but he had to admit that the inspector did not charge the .automobile up to the department?
I claimed he did not.

The hon. gentleman found fault with the inspectors because they spent so much time at the head offices, and he said they were engaged in political work. Be is determined to find fault with these officials; whether they travel around the country in automobiles or stay at the head offices, they are, according to the view of my hon. friend, engaged in political work.
That is what they were appointed for.

The hon. gentleman imputes the most improper motives to these homestead inspectors; he seems to be under the impression that every time they spend a few days at the head offices of the districts they are acting upon some design to help their party. I should imagine that if these gentlemen were really terrorizing the people of the province they would be doing so while making their inspections, thus endeavouring to bring all the pressure they could to bear upon the farmers. They could not meet the farmers by staying in the office at Moosejaw; the hon. gentleman is not very consistent in his arguments.

I never heard anything more lame than the arguments of the minister. If a man steals chickens in Ottawa and sheep in Montreal, iand is found guilty of both offences, would the minister say: how on earth could he steal sheep in Montreal-he has stolen chickens in Ottawa? When these inspectors were at headquarters they were in the committee rooms getting instructions and working on the lists. The minister's explanation of this matter is only a joke. The fact that the country does not pay for the [DOT]automobile in question is the serious part of my charge. If the Government paid for it, that would be the minister's business, but the evidence that has been produced shows conclusively that it was a Conservative automobile. If the minister will go through the diaries, he will find that nobody drove all over the country in an automobile except at election time.
I have no quarrel with the inspectors for travelling expeditiously; I approve of it if the object is to serve the people, but I do say that this is a case where homesteaders, that this is a case where homesteaders, hard up and in great need, were waiting to have their titles straightened out while these gentlemen spent ten or twelve days at a time at headquarters, travelled ninety and a hundred miles at a time, making only four inspections in nineteen days. With this evidence and the other statements I have made, the minister ought to be convinced that these men were engaged in political work at that time. The minister has not given a satisfactory explanation of the matter by any means.
I want to ask the minister whether there is any new regulation of the department which applies to valuable pieces of land adjacent. to towns or cities?

The inspectors have been instructed to make reports upon particularly
valuable quarter-sections adjacent to towns or cities in order that tnese lands may not be thrown open to homestead entry, but may be disposed of by sale, with settlement conditions, or in some other way.
Are there any new regulations with regal'd to valuable quarter sections which were thrown open in 1908?
This regulation applies to all lands that are particularly valuable.
The minister has given instructions, then, that valuable lands adjacent to new towns that may have arisen on a railway line, shall not be available for homestead purposes.
Lands close to towns and cities, which are too valuable to be thrown open to entry, will be disposed of by sale with or without settlement conditions; they will not be open for homestead entry.
Does that mean that there *is to be a system of irregular reservation of homestead entries? If so, who makes the decision as to what reservations shall be made?

For that we have to depend upon our land agents and our inspectors. Certainly in the department we cannot identify a particular parcel of land by the description unless it is brought to out attention that a particular section is sufficiently near a city to render it of special value. This is not a system of irregular reservation; on the contrary, if we were to allow these valuable lands to be thrown open for homestead entry, the hon. member for [DOT]Edmonton would be the first one to make capital against the Government for allowing the free entry of lands that should be reserved to the Crown to be disposed of for purposes of revenue.

The minister has reserved a half section near the town called Goldburg. I presume that has been withdrawn from entry in the way the minister says, that the Dominion land agent in that district has recommended it to him. Has he not had some Dominion land agents whom he has had to get rid of?
Certainly, I have discharged some.	.

I think the minister's
system is one that courts trouble. If he is going to trust some of these land agents such as he has had right in my riding and in other places, and thinks that when such an agent sees a piece of ground that should be reserved he is going to tell the minister instead of his own pal, he is mistaken. The minister was very careful to say that he had not been discourteous to me in connection with the Beaubien investigation. My telegram asked him to advise me when the sittings were to be held and that ^ J might have permission to attend with witnesses. To-night he says he has ordered the investigation and for all I know it may be over. I have not been informed of it and have not had an opportunity of presenting evidence. The Minister has told me that he has not desired to be discourteous. The discussion will be on ' Hansard ' and my constituents will have to judge as to the extent of which he desires to satisfy public opinion as reported to him by their representative. Of course he is the minister, but, after all, I am the representative. The sub land agency at Gravelbourg, one of the busiest in Saskatchewan, was closed up without any reason or explanation being made public. What is the reason for its being closed? Is it because it is a Liberal district and always votes Liberal or is it because my late opponent recommends that it be closed and gives no reason? Is it to punish the people for exercising their franchise? No reason is given on the official file.
Mr. ROCHE The hon. gentleman referred to the fact earlier in the evening that the sub land agent at this point had certain accusations hanging over him in regard to the destruction of the crop of a homesteader. The inspector of land agencies had the sub-agent suspended and reported to tire head office until the charges were cleared up. The office has not as yet been re-

opened. I have had no representations from anybody that I remember for the re-opening of the office. There aTe a number of applications for the opening of new sub land agencies and the re-opening of some that have been closed. They are under consideration. The hon. member's opponent has not recommended the closing of the office and there is no political significance in its closing.

The minister may think so, but he is absolutely wrong. Let him take my word, the office was closed
because this was a Liberal place and the threat was made right and left by prominent Conservatives that it would be closed.
The prominent Conservatives made no such representations to the Minister of the Interior, who is the authority for the closing.
I am making the representation now and people will take it for what it is worth. Has not the office been transferred to another place?
No.

Where are the. files?
ROCHE: There may have been another sub-agency opened some miles away.
Will the minister reopen the office in Gravelbourg if he can hnd a suitable sub-agent?

That depends on the
amount of land in the vicinity to be taken up and the public requirements.
Will the minister tell me if I can call witnesses in the case we discussed?

The file was sent out West to the inspector of land agencies, so that he may take evidence under oath; but the investigation is not being prosecuted at the present time. The file had to be brought back to this city in order to respond to the hon. gentleman's motion and it is here now; so it is not likely that any investigation will be carried on in the immediate future. If the hon. gentleman desires to be present at the investigation I have not the slightest objection.
Will you see that I am notified when it is to be held?
Yes.
Will you give instructions that I may call witnesses?

Certainly, if desired.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 12.15 a.m. Friday.
Friday, March 20, 1914.
